**A Message About Math Class Changes**

Dear Parents and Caregivers,

We’re writing to explain a change we’re making in how we teach math. Starting next year, your child will no longer be placed in separate “fast,” “middle,” or “slow” math groups. Instead, all students will learn math together in the same classroom, with extra support built in for those who need it.

We know this is a big change, and you may have questions or worries. Please read this – we want to be open and honest about why we’re doing this and what it means for your child.

**The old way: sorting kids by “ability”**

In the past, we tested students and put them into groups based on how quickly they seemed to learn math. We called this “streaming” or “tracking.”

The problem? This system often hurt more than it helped.

- **It held many kids back.** Students in the “lower” group often got easier, repetitive work. They fell further behind because they weren’t challenged to think deeply. They also started to believe they were “just not good at math.”
- **It wasn’t fair.** Kids develop at different speeds. A child who struggled in September might have caught up by January, but they were stuck in the “slow” group all year. Also, children from poorer families or certain backgrounds were far more likely to be placed in lower groups – not because they couldn’t do math, but because of bias or lack of extra help at home.
- **It made math feel lonely and scary.** When kids are separated, they lose the chance to learn from each other. And being labeled “behind” can make a child give up.

**The new way: learning together, with support**

Now, we’re moving to what’s called **mixed-attainment teaching**. That means every student in a grade learns the same big math ideas together. But we don’t teach everyone the same way.

Here’s what actually happens in the classroom:

- **The teacher teaches the whole class together** – explaining a new concept, like fractions or algebra, step by step.
- **Then, students work in small groups or pairs.** These groups change often. Sometimes they’re mixed (a student who finds math easy works with a student who finds it hard). Sometimes they’re grouped by a specific skill for a short time (like extra practice on multiplication tables).
- **Extra help is given right away.** If a student is confused, the teacher or a teaching assistant works with them immediately – not weeks later. We also use hands-on tools, pictures, and real-life examples so every child can understand.
- **Everyone is challenged.** Students who catch on quickly get harder problems and deeper questions – not just more of the same. They might be asked to explain *why* a method works or to find a different way to solve a problem.

**Why this is better for your child**

Research from around the world shows that mixed-attainment teaching helps **all** students – not just some.

- **Students learn more.** When kids explain ideas to each other, they understand them better. The student who “gets it” strengthens their own knowledge by teaching. The student who is struggling hears it in a different way from a peer.
- **Confidence grows.** No one is labeled “dumb” or “smart.” Every child sees themselves as a learner who can improve with effort. This is huge – kids who believe they can get better actually do get better.
- **It mirrors real life.** In jobs and families, we work with people of all different skills. Learning to work with others, ask for help, and explain your thinking is a life skill – not just a math skill.
- **It closes gaps.** In the old system, the gap between the “top” and “bottom” groups grew every year. In mixed classes, that gap shrinks. More students leave school ready for college, trade school, or work.

**What about my child who is “good” at math? Won’t they be held back?**

We understand this worry. But the truth is, in the old system, many “top” students were just good at memorizing steps. They never learned to think deeply. In a mixed class, your child will still be challenged – but in a richer way. They’ll be asked to solve puzzles, prove their answers, and explore multiple methods. They’ll also learn patience and empathy – skills that help in every career.

**What about my child who struggles? Won’t they feel lost or embarrassed?**

We will never leave a child to sink or swim. We are adding more support staff, smaller group work, and extra practice time. And we will watch each child closely. If your child is truly struggling with a basic skill (like counting or times tables), we will give them extra help – sometimes in a small group for a short time – but they will still come back to the main class. The goal is to keep them included, not to hide them away.

**We need your help**

This change works best when we work together. Here’s what you can do at home:

- **Talk positively about math.** Say things like, “I’m not sure how to do this, but let’s figure it out together.” Never say, “I was bad at math too” – that gives your child permission to give up.
- **Ask your child to teach you.** Ask, “What did you learn in math today? Can you show me?” This builds their confidence.
- **Be patient.** It may take a few months for your child to adjust. Some children may feel frustrated at first because they’re not used to explaining their thinking. That’s normal.

**We want to hear from you**

We know you love your child and want what’s best. We do too. This change is not easy for teachers – it takes more planning and skill. But we believe it is the right thing for every child.

Please come to our parent information night on **[date]** at **[time]** in the school hall. We’ll show you examples of lessons, answer your questions, and listen to your concerns. You can also call the school office or email **[teacher’s name]** at **[email]** .

Thank you for trusting us with your child’s education. We are committed to making sure every student – including yours – leaves our school feeling capable, confident, and ready for the future.

Sincerely,
